items.title: 14.3.7 Real World Applications on Cross or Vector Product

blocks.text: If \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are two non-zero vectors and \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\), then \(|\underline{u}|\) and \(|\underline{v}|\) represent the length of the adjacent sides of a parallelogram (see figure). We know that

blocks.alt: Vectors u and v from a common corner with the angle between them marked; the other two sides of the parallelogram are dashed. A dotted line from the tip of u straight down to v is labelled h = |u| sin theta. The sides are labelled |u| and |v|.
blocks.caption: Figure: parallelogram on u and v with height h = |u| sin θ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why \(h = |\underline{u}|\sin\theta\): the height drops perpendicular from the tip of \(\underline{u}\) to the base \(\underline{v}\). In that right triangle the hypotenuse is \(|\underline{u}|\) and \(h\) is opposite \(\theta\), so \(\sin\theta = h/|\underline{u}|\). With base \(|\underline{v}|\): area \(= |\underline{v}|\,|\underline{u}|\sin\theta = |\underline{u} \times \underline{v}|\).

From figure it is clear that
\[\text{Area of triangle} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{Area of parallelogram})\]
\[\text{Area of triangle} = \tfrac{1}{2}|\underline{u} \times \underline{v}|\]
where \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are vectors along two adjacent sides of the triangle.

blocks.alt: Vectors u and v from a common corner with the angle between them marked; the parallelogram on them is completed with dashed lines, and a dashed diagonal joins the tips of u and v, cutting it into two equal triangles. The sides are labelled |u| and |v|.
blocks.caption: Figure: the triangle on u and v is half of the parallelogram (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: For a triangle given by its vertices \(A, B, C\): take two sides from the same vertex, e.g. \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}\); then area \(= \tfrac12|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}|\). For a parallelogram, make sure the two vectors are adjacent sides, not a side and a diagonal.

blocks.title: Example 20
blocks.problem: Find area of the parallelogram whose vertices are \(P(0, 0, 0)\), \(Q(-1, 2, 4)\), \(R(2, -1, 4)\) and \(S(1, 1, 8)\).
steps:
Given: \(P(0, 0, 0)\), \(Q(-1, 2, 4)\), \(R(2, -1, 4)\), \(S(1, 1, 8)\).
To find: the area of the parallelogram.
Method: area \(= |\overrightarrow{PQ} \times \overrightarrow{PR}|\) with \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\), \(\overrightarrow{PR}\) adjacent sides. (Indeed \(Q + R - P = (1, 1, 8) = S\), so \(S\) is the vertex opposite \(P\).)

Step 1: The side vectors
\[\overrightarrow{PQ} = (-1 - 0)\underline{i} + (2 - 0)\underline{j} + (4 - 0)\underline{k}\]
\[= -\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} + 4\underline{k}\]
\[\overrightarrow{PR} = (2 - 0)\underline{i} + (-1 - 0)\underline{j} + (4 - 0)\underline{k}\]
\[= 2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + 4\underline{k}\]
Why: \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{OQ} - \overrightarrow{OP}\): end point minus start point.

Step 3: The area
\[|12\underline{i} + 12\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}| = \sqrt{144 + 144 + 9}\]
\[= \sqrt{297} = 3\sqrt{33}\]
Why: the area is the length of the cross product; \(297 = 9 \times 33\).

Check:
\[(12, 12, -3) \cdot (-1, 2, 4) = -12 + 24 - 12 = 0\]
\[(12, 12, -3) \cdot (2, -1, 4) = 24 - 12 - 12 = 0\]
The cross product is perpendicular to both sides, so the working is consistent.

blocks.title: Example 21
blocks.problem: Find the area of the triangle with vertices \(A(1, -1, 1)\), \(B(2, 1, -1)\) and \(C(-1, 1, 2)\). Also find a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of triangle \(ABC\).
steps:
Given: \(A(1, -1, 1)\), \(B(2, 1, -1)\), \(C(-1, 1, 2)\).
To find: the area of triangle \(ABC\) and a unit vector perpendicular to its plane.
Method: \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), \(\overrightarrow{AC}\) are adjacent sides; area \(= \tfrac12|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}|\), and \(\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}\) is normal to the plane.

Step 1: The side vectors
\[\overrightarrow{AB} = (2 - 1)\underline{i} + (1 + 1)\underline{j} + (-1 - 1)\underline{k}\]
\[= \underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - 2\underline{k}\]
\[\overrightarrow{AC} = (-1 - 1)\underline{i} + (1 + 1)\underline{j} + (2 - 1)\underline{k}\]
\[= -2\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} + \underline{k}\]
Why: end point minus start point; \(1 - (-1) = 1 + 1\).

Step 3: Area of the parallelogram on these sides
\[|6\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}| = \sqrt{36 + 9 + 36}\]
\[= \sqrt{81} = 9\]
Why: this is the parallelogram's area; the triangle is half of it.

Step 4: Area of the triangle
\[\tfrac12|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}| = \tfrac{9}{2}\]
Why: a diagonal cuts the parallelogram into two equal triangles.

Step 5: The unit vector
\[\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}}{|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}|} = \dfrac{1}{9}(6\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 6\underline{k})\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{3}(2\underline{i} + \underline{j} + 2\underline{k})\]
Why: divide by the length 9, then take out the common factor 3.

Check:
\[\tfrac13(2 + 2 - 4) = 0,\quad \tfrac13(-4 + 2 + 2) = 0\]
\[\tfrac13\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 1\]
Zero dot products with \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}\), and length 1. The opposite vector \(-\tfrac13(2\underline{i} + \underline{j} + 2\underline{k})\) is equally valid.
blocks.answer: Area \(= \frac{9}{2}\) square units; unit vector \(\frac13(2\underline{i} + \underline{j} + 2\underline{k})\) (or its negative).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 21 the coordinates of vertex \(B\) are printed with damaged characters; the book's own solution uses \(B(2, 1, -1)\), which we use here. In the last line the printed equality signs look like minus signs; the result is \(\frac{1}{9}(6\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}) = \frac{1}{3}(2\underline{i} + \underline{j} + 2\underline{k})\).

Let a force \(\underline{F}\,(\overrightarrow{PQ})\) act at a point \(P\) as shown in the figure, then moment of \(\underline{F}\) about \(O\)
= Product of force \(\underline{F}\) and perpendicular ON the direction of \(\underline{n}\)
\[= (PQ)(ON)(\underline{n})\]
\[= (PQ)(OP)\sin\theta\,(\underline{n})\]
\[= \overrightarrow{OP} \times \overrightarrow{PQ} = \underline{r} \times \underline{F}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The wording of this line is garbled in print. It should read: moment of \(\underline{F}\) about \(O\) = (magnitude of the force \(\underline{F}\)) × (the perpendicular distance \(ON\) from \(O\) to the line of action of \(\underline{F}\)), in the direction of the unit vector \(\underline{n}\).

blocks.alt: Point O above a horizontal line through N, P and Q. ON is dashed and perpendicular to the line, and NP is dashed. Vector r runs from O to P and is produced beyond P; the force F acts along PQ. The angle theta is marked at P between PQ and the extension of r, and again between PN and PO. The vector r cross F is drawn upward from O.
blocks.caption: Figure: moment of the force F about O, with r = OP and ON perpendicular to the line of action (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why \(ON = OP\sin\theta\): triangle \(ONP\) has a right angle at \(N\), and the angle at \(P\) between \(PO\) and \(PN\) equals \(\theta\) (vertically opposite to the angle between \(\underline{r}\) extended and \(\underline{F}\)). So \(\sin\theta = ON/OP\).
Hence \(|\underline{r} \times \underline{F}| = |\underline{r}||\underline{F}|\sin\theta\) is force × perpendicular distance, the familiar moment (torque) from Physics, and \(\underline{r} \times \underline{F}\) also gives its direction (the axis of turning).
Order matters: the moment is \(\underline{r} \times \underline{F}\), with \(\underline{r}\) drawn from the point \(O\) to the line of action.

blocks.title: Example 22
blocks.problem: Find the moment about the point \(M(-2, 4, -6)\) of the force represented by \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), where coordinates of points \(A\) and \(B\) are \((1, 2, -3)\) and \((3, -4, 2)\) respectively.
steps:
Given: \(M(-2, 4, -6)\), \(A(1, 2, -3)\), \(B(3, -4, 2)\); the force is \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
To find: the moment of the force about \(M\), and its magnitude.
Method: moment \(= \underline{r} \times \underline{F}\) with \(\underline{F} = \overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\underline{r}\) from \(M\) to a point of the line of action; \(A\) lies on it, so \(\underline{r} = \overrightarrow{MA}\).

Step 1: The force vector
\[\overrightarrow{AB} = (3 - 1)\underline{i} + (-4 - 2)\underline{j} + (2 + 3)\underline{k}\]
\[= 2\underline{i} - 6\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\]
Why: \(B\) minus \(A\).

Step 3: The moment
\[\underline{r} \times \underline{F} = \overrightarrow{MA} \times \overrightarrow{AB}\]
\[= \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 3 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & -6 & 5 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (-10 + 18)\underline{i} - (15 - 6)\underline{j} + (-18 + 4)\underline{k}\]
\[= 8\underline{i} - 9\underline{j} - 14\underline{k}\]
Why: the order is \(\underline{r} \times \underline{F}\), so \(\overrightarrow{MA}\) goes in row 2.

Step 4: Its magnitude
\[|\underline{r} \times \underline{F}| = \sqrt{8^{2} + (-9)^{2} + (-14)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{64 + 81 + 196} = \sqrt{341}\]
Why: the magnitude formula.

Check:
\[\overrightarrow{MB} = 5\underline{i} - 8\underline{j} + 8\underline{k}\]
\[\overrightarrow{MB} \times \overrightarrow{AB} = 8\underline{i} - 9\underline{j} - 14\underline{k}\]
Using the other point \(B\) of the line gives the same moment, because \(\overrightarrow{MB} = \overrightarrow{MA} + \overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AB} = \underline{0}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Area of parallelogram with adjacent sides \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}\) \(= |\underline{u} \times \underline{v}|\).
2. Area of triangle \(= \tfrac12|\underline{u} \times \underline{v}|\), with \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}\) along two sides from one vertex.
3. Moment of \(\underline{F}\) about \(O\) \(= \underline{r} \times \underline{F}\), \(\underline{r}\) from \(O\) to any point of the line of action.
4. The magnitude of the moment is force × perpendicular distance.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the \(\tfrac12\) for a triangle.
2. Using a diagonal instead of an adjacent side for the parallelogram.
3. Writing \(\underline{F} \times \underline{r}\) for the moment: this gives the opposite direction.
4. Taking \(\underline{r}\) from the line to the point (\(\overrightarrow{AM}\) instead of \(\overrightarrow{MA}\)): this also reverses the sign.
